common.sourceSection: Why these screens are not the real ones
common.clickHint: Click any box to open that screen; click the empty canvas to enlarge the diagram.
common.source: `Chat.stories.tsx`, `Presence.stories.tsx` and `chat-parts.tsx` rebuild the **layout** from `@noalhub/ui` primitives instead of importing `apps/web/components/chat/*`: the apps are built and deployed independently and may not import across each other, and the real components need `@noalhub/api` hooks plus a live Socket.IO connection to render at all. Change the real components without changing these stories and the map drifts. The rules behind every step live in `docs/chat.md`.
common.redisSection: Redis — where the state actually lives
common.blogSource: This page documents `packages/api/src/blog/server.ts`, `apps/web/app/api/revalidate/route.ts` and `apps/admin/components/posts/post-editor.tsx` — it does not rebuild them. The boxes in the flow map link to the `UI/Blog` component stories, which are the real components from `@noalhub/ui`. The full rules, including the parts the backend owns, live in `docs/blog.md`.

chat.title: The chat flow
chat.lead: Two views of the same thing. The **flow map** says which states a user moves through; the **sequence** says what each of those steps says to the backend.
chat.flowCaption: The two loops are design decisions, not decoration: **retry** goes back to the very same send step with the very same `id`, and **reconnect** has to pass through an invalidate before the conversation is trustworthy again.
chat.seqCaption: Read top to bottom. Left of the dashed line is the frontend, right of it is the backend.

edges.backoff: Socket.IO backs off on its own

steps.4: connect() — only once auth has bootstrapped
steps.5: handshake /socket.io/ · auth: { token }, never in the query string
steps.6: BE joins user:{id} + conv:{…} from the DB — the FE emits no join
steps.9: 200 MessagePageDto · items NEWEST FIRST, nextCursor is a uuid
steps.10: submit → onMutate: insert { id: uuidv7(), status: sending }
steps.11: emit message:send { id, conversationId, body } · 10s timeout
steps.12: ack { ok: true, message } → upsertById → sent
steps.13: message:new + conversation:updated → setQueryData, dedupe by id
steps.14: emit message:mark-read (offline falls back to POST /{id}/read)
steps.15: disconnect → after reconnect you MUST invalidate both queries

notes.1: **Steps 2–3 and 8–9 are REST, and READ-ONLY.** There is no `POST /messages` — the backend deliberately keeps **one** write path.
notes.2: **Steps 11–12 are that single write path**, drawn in the accent colour. The composer therefore depends on the socket: losing the connection means losing the ability to send, not merely sending slowly.
notes.3: **The `id` the FE mints at step 10** (UUID v7) is the backend's idempotency key: resending the same `id` hits a PK conflict and the backend returns the original row. Retrying is completely safe, and no separate `clientId` is needed.
notes.4: **Step 13 can land BEFORE step 12.** Your own `message:new` and the ack are independent paths; both `upsertById`, so either order yields one message.
notes.5: **Step 6: the FE never emits join/subscribe.** Rooms are assigned by the backend from DB membership — it explicitly never trusts a `conversationId` sent by a client.
notes.6: **Step 15 is where messages go missing.** The socket only carries events from connect onwards, so after a reconnect you must invalidate both `conversations` and `messages`. Without those two lines, 30 seconds offline means lost messages and a UI that says nothing.
notes.7: **Steps 3 and 9 carry presence along.** `members[].status` is a presence snapshot and is seeded straight into the ephemeral store — see the Flows/Presence page.
notes.8: **The two read endpoints use two different cursors**: the conversation list a `date-time`, message history a `uuid`. One shared `getNextPageParam` is a type error on sight.
notes.9: **404 covers both “does not exist” and “not a member”.** The backend deliberately will not reveal whether a conversation is real → do not build a 403 branch, it would be dead forever.

presence.title: Presence — online / offline
presence.lead: Presence has **no endpoint of its own**. It reaches the app two ways: a snapshot riding along on the chat REST responses (`members[].status`), and after that `presence:changed` events on the socket. Both land in one zustand store — no React Query, no ack.
presence.flowCaption: **Two states, and offline is the one you start in.** The store can hold nothing at all for a user, and the UI renders that absence as offline — so the dot is never blank and never a third colour. The seed is what turns it green before any event arrives.
presence.seqCaption: The same two states seen along the data path: which hop is REST and which is a socket event.

edges.noData: no entry at all → still offline

steps.1: useConversations() / useConversation() — the chat flow's REST, not a presence API
steps.2: members[].status + lastSeenAt — a presence snapshot as of the response
steps.3: useSeedPresence(): setPresence for every member that HAS a status
steps.4: green / grey dot on the very first render, no event needed
steps.5: member.status === null (the list only computes it for DMs) or an unseen userId
steps.6: usePresence → undefined, and the view renders that as OFFLINE
steps.7: the other person opens the app · handshake /socket.io/
steps.8: presence:changed { userId, status: online } — only to people who share a conversation
steps.11: closes the tab / loses the network
steps.12: presence:changed { status: offline, lastSeenAt } — usually ~1 second
steps.13: a backend instance dies abruptly: offline lags UP TO 60 SECONDS (staleAfter)
steps.14: reconnect → invalidate conversations → refetch → seeded again (steps 1–3)

notes.1: **Two states, and “we have not heard” is drawn as offline.** Presence is only broadcast to people who share a conversation, so the store is empty for everyone else. The product decides a reader cannot act on the difference between “away” and “unknown”, so there is no third dot.
notes.2: **The cost of that, so it is not rediscovered as a bug:** someone who is genuinely online reads as offline until the first fact about them arrives. Which makes step 3 load-bearing rather than an optimisation.
notes.3: **Steps 1–4: presence is seeded from REST, not only from the socket.** `useSeedPresence()` reads `members[].status` off `useConversations` / `useConversation` and writes it straight into the store. Without it an online peer stays grey, because `presence:changed` only fires on a **change** — it never announces the current state.
notes.4: **`status: null` is still skipped by the seed** (steps 5–6). It means the endpoint did not compute presence, not that the person is away, so the store keeps no entry rather than writing a value the backend never sent. The collapse to offline happens in the **view**, which is what keeps that decision in one file.
notes.5: **Step 13: offline can lag by up to 60 seconds** when a backend instance dies abruptly (`staleAfter = 60s`). The normal exits — closing the tab, losing the network — stay around 1 second. Do not build UI that depends on instant presence.
notes.6: **Step 14: a reconnect heals presence by itself.** There is no presence API to refetch, but the invalidate required after every reconnect pulls `conversations` back and the snapshot in that response re-runs the seed.
notes.7: **Colour alone communicates nothing.** The dot always ships a `title` plus `sr-only` text, so the two states are told apart by words and not only by shade.

presence.redisCaption: The same two states seen from the backend: online/offline is **not** a Postgres column but **two sorted sets in Redis**. Postgres only keeps `users.last_seen_at`, written at the moment a user goes offline and never otherwise.

redisKeys.userPurpose: Online = `ZCOUNT` over `(now−60s, +inf)` > 0. The 24h `EXPIRE` only stops a user who never comes back from leaving a key behind — it is **not** how offline is detected.
redisKeys.expiryShape: Global ZSET — member = `{userId}:{socketId}`, score = last heartbeat
redisKeys.expiryPurpose: The index the reaper walks. Without it, finding dead sockets means `SCAN presence:*` — O(users) every 5 seconds even when nobody just went offline.
redisKeys.reaperShape: `SET NX PX` — TTL of half a reap tick (2.5s)
redisKeys.reaperPurpose: Keeps one tick to one instance; otherwise every offline fires N duplicate events. The lock expires, so a dead instance cannot hold it forever.

redisSteps.1: the peer opens the app · /socket.io/ handshake
redisSteps.2: connect(userId, socketId) — all three calls below are ONE Lua script
redisSteps.3: ZADD presence:{userId} score=now member=socketId · EXPIRE 24h · ZREMRANGEBYSCORE drops this user's stale sockets
redisSteps.5: ZCARD = 1 → the user JUST went from offline to online (in-script, so two tabs opened at once cannot both read 1)
redisSteps.6: presence:changed { status: online } — only to people sharing a conversation
redisSteps.7: every 20 seconds (REFRESH_MS): refresh the score of THIS instance's own sockets
redisSteps.8: same tick, same score — let the two keys drift and they disagree on which socket is alive
redisSteps.9: tab closed / reload / network lost → disconnect(userId, socketId)
redisSteps.10: ZADD XX score = now + 8s − 60s → expires in exactly the 8s grace. NO offline is published here
redisSteps.11: every 5 seconds: SET presence:reaper NX PX 2500 — lose the lock, skip this tick
redisSteps.12: ZRANGEBYSCORE ≤ now−60s → ZREM; only the instance whose ZREM removed it carries on
redisSteps.13: ZCOUNT: no fresh socket left for this user → only now is it really offline
redisSteps.14: UPDATE users.last_seen_at — the only time presence touches the DB
redisSteps.15: presence:changed { status: offline, lastSeenAt } — the ONLY place offline is published

redisNotes.1: **Steps 7 and 13 are where the 60 seconds comes from.** Scores are refreshed every 20s and counted dead after 60s (≈ 3 ticks, so one tick lost to a GC pause never reports a false offline). When a BE instance dies outright nothing refreshes them — so the dot goes grey **after up to 60 seconds**.
redisNotes.2: **Step 10 is why a reload does not flicker.** `disconnect` publishes nothing; it only lowers the score to “expires in 8 seconds” (`PRESENCE_GRACE_MS`). The reload's new socket lands inside that window, the reaper sees a fresh socket and **says nothing at all**. The cost: a genuinely closed tab reads offline after ~8–13s, not ~1s.
redisNotes.3: **Leaving is a lowered score, never a `ZREM`** — and via `ZADD XX`, which only touches members that still exist. A plain `ZADD` would resurrect a socket the reaper just removed and keep the user in the index for another round.
redisNotes.4: **Offline is published only by the reaper (steps 11–15), never by `disconnect`.** One exit means one place that can get it wrong — and duplicates are ruled out by the `ZREM` result rather than by the lock, since a broken lock only costs a double sweep.
redisNotes.5: **The 5s reap tick is deliberately separate from the 20s refresh tick.** Fold them together and the 8-second grace still has to wait for the next 20-second tick — a closed tab would take up to 28 seconds to read offline.
redisNotes.6: **Running more than one BE instance without Redis fails silently.** `PresenceStore` has an in-memory implementation for single-instance setups; from the second instance on, `RedisPresenceStore` is required **together with** `@socket.io/redis-adapter`. On the FE it shows up as presence and messages “only working when you get lucky” — that is not an FE bug.
redisNotes.7: **This whole diagram is backend.** The FE reads no Redis, has no presence endpoint, and can fix none of this latency. It is in Storybook because every number the UI has to live with — 60 seconds, 8 seconds — is produced by exactly these steps.

states.offlineNote: status: offline + lastSeenAt — or no entry in the store at all

blog.title: Blog flow — from a draft to a public page
blog.lead: The blog is the **only** feature that reads through a fourth layer: `server.ts`, running in `apps/web`'s Server Components with no token at all. Public posts need no auth, and for SEO fetching on the server is not "nicer" but **required** — client rendering leaves the first HTML empty. The price is a cache, and the whole flow below is about who clears it and when.
blog.flowCaption: A post has **four** states, and only one of them is visible to the public. The two dead ends are deliberate: **archived** is a soft delete, and an **old slug** never disappears — it keeps answering, with a redirect.

nodes.publishedNote: in the list, sitemap and RSS
nodes.unpublishedNote: back to `draft` · gone from the site

blog.seqCaption: Pressing Publish and seeing the post are **two** chains, and the only thing joining them is step 4. Drop that webhook and nothing breaks — the page just stays stale for up to 60 seconds (`revalidate` is the safety net, not the mechanism).

steps.6: 200 `{ revalidated: true }` — a failure here is swallowed and logged
steps.8: cache lookup → miss, the tag was just expired
steps.12: store the response under its tags
steps.13: HTML rendered on the server — full text in the first response

blog.slugCaption: Renaming a slug does not move the post — it **adds** a row to the slug history. The old URL keeps working forever, which is why the backend has to revalidate both slugs: the old one is still cached under its own tag.

slugSteps.3: miss on `slug`, hit on the slug-history table
slugSteps.7: the post, this time with no redirect

blog.cacheCaption: Every `fetch` in `server.ts` carries a tag, and `POST /api/revalidate` **builds the tag names itself** from the slugs it is handed — the body never carries a tag name or a path. Otherwise the endpoint becomes a tool for re-rendering any route in the app.

tags.listPurpose: Cleared on publish, unpublish/archive, and on editing an already-published post. One tag covers `?page=1`, `?page=2`, … which is exactly why `revalidatePath` is unusable.
tags.postPurpose: One tag per slug. A rename sends **both** the old and the new — the old slug is still cached under its own tag and still serving.
tags.categoryPurpose: Moving a post to another category sends **both** categories. Send only the new one and the old category page keeps listing the post for another 300 seconds.
tags.tagPurpose: Same rule: **both** the old and the new set of tags. Removing a tag without revalidating it leaves `/blogs/tag/<old>` listing a post that no longer carries it.
tags.categoriesPurpose: The public `postCount` changes on publish/unpublish/move — and so does any category CRUD, because renaming a category changes the cached title of `/blogs/category/<slug>`.
tags.tagsPurpose: Cleared when the first post takes a new tag, or the last post drops one — that is when the tag index itself changes, not just a listing.
tags.sitemapPurpose: Every change of published state. It feeds `sitemap.xml`, `rss.xml` and `generateStaticParams`; miss it and Google keeps being pointed at a post that is gone.

notes.1: **The caller must be the backend, never `apps/admin`.** Admin is code in a browser: putting the secret there publishes it, and calling without one hands anyone a DoS lever — each request forces `web` to drop its cache, re-render and call back into the backend. With the backend calling at the exact point it writes `status`, every path that publishes a post — button, seed script, a future sync job — revalidates, with none missed.
notes.2: **`{ expire: 0 }`, not `"max"`.** `"max"` is stale-while-revalidate, so the first F5 after Publish would still show the old version — which is the one thing this whole chain exists to prevent. `updateTag` has the right semantics but only works inside a Server Action, never a Route Handler.
notes.3: **The webhook is the fast path, not the only one.** `revalidate` is 60s for the list, 300s for a post, 3600s for the taxonomy pages. If the webhook is lost the site still corrects itself; the failure mode is a delay, never wrong data. That is also why the backend swallows a webhook error instead of failing the publish.
notes.4: **The ISR cache lives inside each container.** One `web` container today, so this is fine. The day it becomes two replicas, one webhook refreshes exactly one of them and the other keeps serving the old page until its `revalidate` expires — at which point a shared cache handler is needed.
notes.5: **404 and "the API blipped" must never merge.** `server.ts` returns `null` on 404 so the route can call `notFound()`, and **throws** on everything else for `error.tsx`. Swap the two and either Google drops real posts because the API hiccuped once, or it keeps retrying a URL that does not exist.
notes.6: **`generateStaticParams` must never redden the build.** CI builds the image on a GitHub runner where `API_INTERNAL_URL` does not exist, so `server.ts` falls back to the public URL and `next build` calls the production API. It is wrapped in a `try/catch` returning `[]` — `dynamicParams` is `true`, so posts still render on demand. Every deploy starts with an empty cache anyway, so prerendering only ever saved the first visit.
notes.7: **`/blogs` is dynamic and that is not a misconfiguration.** Reading `searchParams.page` opts the route out of static rendering, so `export const revalidate` on the page does nothing. The caching that matters happens one level down, on the `fetch` inside `server.ts`.
notes.8: **Pagination has to be real `<a href>`.** Googlebot runs JS but does not click buttons, so a `onPageChange` pagination leaves no crawl path past page 1. Posts still get indexed via the sitemap; what is lost is the internal linking, and sitemap-only URLs rank lower.
notes.9: **Three slugs are forbidden:** `category`, `tag`, `rss.xml`. They are static segments beside `/blogs/[slug]`, and Next always lets a static segment win — a post given one of those slugs would be permanently unreachable. The backend rejects them at validation time.
notes.10: **The editor saves only on click — there is no autosave, not even for drafts.** One copy of the content, edited live, which means editing a published post edits what the public is reading right now, and a power cut loses the work. In exchange no half-finished version ever reaches the public on its own. `version` + a 409 is what stops two tabs from overwriting each other.

sample.author: Noah Pham
sample.p1Title: Why the blog reads through a fourth layer
sample.p1Excerpt: Public posts need no token, so they can be fetched on the server — and for SEO that is not an optimisation but a requirement.
sample.p2Title: Publish, and the page is already there
sample.p2Excerpt: The backend rings the bell after it commits. Sixty seconds of ISR is the safety net underneath, not the mechanism.
sample.p3Excerpt: Two paths, one tag — which is the whole reason revalidatePath never made it into this feature.
sample.p4Excerpt: Renaming does not move a post. It forks a row into the slug history, and the old URL keeps answering with a 308 forever.
sample.p5Excerpt: Categories are navigation and get indexed; tags are cross-links and do not. Collapsing them into one list loses both jobs.
sample.p6Title: The editor that refuses to autosave
sample.p6Excerpt: One copy of the content, saved on click. The cost is a power cut; the prize is that no half-written paragraph ever ships itself.
sample.docIntro: A post is not one cached thing but several: the listing that mentions it, its own page, its category, each of its tags, and the sitemap that points at it.
sample.docBodyA: The route handler builds every tag name itself, from the slugs in the body. Nothing in the request names a tag or a path.
sample.docBodyB: The old slug is still cached under a tag of its own, and it is still serving. Revalidate only the new one and the old URL answers from yesterday.
sample.docH2B: Where the sixty seconds comes from
sample.docBodyC: `revalidate` is the floor, not the plan. If the webhook is lost the site still corrects itself; the failure mode is delay, never wrong data.
